explanations: terra: The God-conscious establish prayer and spend from provision, while 2:4 completes their portrait with certainty in the Hereafter.
terra: Certainty in the Hereafter supplies the account-facing stance for the prayer and spending named in 2:3.

luna: The section gathers care for vulnerable people, prayer, and zakah into a broken circle; this covenant joins worship, care for orphans and poor people, good speech, prayer, and zakah, then notes that most turned away. | terra: One covenant joins worship of God, kindness to orphans and the needy, good speech, prayer, and zakat, gathering nearly every link whose dissolution the section traces.
terra: Prayer and zakat are followed by the assurance that every good sent ahead is found with God and that God sees what people do, opposing worship for human eyes.

luna: The Al-Alaq scene in the section is about obstructing a praying servant; this ayah broadens that boundary to those who prevent God's name from being remembered in mosques and work for their ruin. | terra: The one who prevents God's name being mentioned in places of worship and strives to ruin them parallels the prayer-obstructor in 96:9-10 and receives disgrace and punishment.

luna: The section's disconnected prayer, orphan, poor, and denial are gathered here into *birr*: giving to kin, orphans, and poor, establishing prayer, giving zakah, and believing in the Last Day belong to one truthful pattern. | terra: Righteousness is denied to a mere facing posture and defined through the Last Day, giving wealth to orphans and the needy, prayer, and zakat—the full positive structure behind the section's critique.

luna: The section pictures the orphan as pushed outside protection; this ayah says “إِصْلَاحٌ لَّهُمْ خَيْرٌ” and calls orphans brothers when they share a household, replacing expulsion with care and fellowship. | terra: Setting orphan affairs right is declared best, and sharing life with them makes them brothers; household inclusion answers expulsion at the door.

luna: The section's lexicographic reading of ma'un includes a small thing lent or owed; this verse calls giving wealth for God's cause “قَرْضًا حَسَنًا,” a distinct, metaphorical loan that extends the image from neighborly aid to accountable giving. | terra: A good loan to God is multiplied, and God constricts and expands provision before return to Him; debt, provision, and final repayment meet directly.
terra: A kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury, giving the mouth at the needy person's door a positive role even when material aid is absent.

luna: The section contrasts attention-seeking prayer with neglected need; this ayah shows ostentatious charity “رِئَاءَ النَّاسِ” that leaves no lasting benefit when rain strips a rock bare, so being seen does not itself feed anyone. | terra: The giver who spends رِئَاءَ النَّاسِ while disbelieving in God and the Last Day makes charity into the same spectator-facing surface as the section's prayer.
terra: Those who spend seeking God's pleasure and inward certainty are compared to a fruitful garden, the intention-level opposite of the show-giver in 2:264.
terra: A man with weak offspring loses a rivered garden to a fiery whirlwind, bringing dependent children, water, provision, and fire into one warning scene.

luna: The section's prayer is done for human eyes, but this ayah draws a specific boundary: open charity is good, while concealing it and giving it to the poor is better, distinguishing visibility from its purpose and recipient. | terra: Open charity is allowed, but hidden charity to the poor is better; the ayah draws the boundary between visibility itself and spectator-seeking display.
terra: Whatever wealth is spent seeking God's face returns fully to the giver, joining pure intention to repayment without wrong.

luna: The section says needy people are overlooked as faint; this verse describes poor people whose restraint makes the uninformed think they are self-sufficient, though they can be recognized by their signs and do not persistently ask. | terra: The restrained poor are thought rich because they do not beg insistently and must be recognized by their mark; they are precisely the faint, easily missed needy person in the section's visual field.
terra: Those who spend by night and day, secretly and openly, show that visible giving need not be riyā when the act remains accountable to God.
terra: A debtor in hardship must be given respite, and remission as charity is better; this states the mercy due at the small-debt end of the image.
terra: Immediately before the debt rule, a Day is feared when every soul returns to God and is paid in full, joining worldly obligation to final settlement.
terra: The d-y-n wording shifts from judgment to literal debt: write a debt to its term and do not tire of recording it, whether small or large, so the source's account and small debt fully meet.
terra: The trusted person must discharge the trust entrusted to him and fear God, directly governing a borrowed household object when no written record is available.
terra: Those stingy with God's bounty will have what they withheld made a collar on Resurrection, turning the closed hand into a visible bond at account.

luna: The section says an orphan has lost a protective circle; this verse makes the guardian's concrete duty to deliver orphans' property and not consume it part of that protection. | terra: The command to give orphans their property and not consume it makes the orphan's due inviolable rather than something a stronger hand may push aside.

luna: Continuing the orphan-care rules, this ayah requires testing until maturity and handing over property when judgment is sound; it specifies how a guardian preserves what belongs to the child. | terra: Guardians must test orphans, deliver their property, avoid consuming it, and call witnesses; وَكَفَى بِاللَّهِ حَسِيبًا joins protection of the due to divine accounting.
terra: When orphans and the needy attend a division, they are to receive something and hear kind words, a direct refusal to let the faint person at the edge leave empty-handed.
terra: Guardians are told to imagine leaving weak offspring behind, fear for them, and speak rightly, articulating the protective circle the source's orphan lacks.

luna: The section joins an orphan's treatment to fire; this verse makes that bond concrete in another way, saying those who unjustly consume orphans' property “إِنَّمَا يَأْكُلُونَ فِي بُطُونِهِمْ نَارًا.” | terra: Those who consume orphan property eat fire into their bellies and سَيَصْلَوْنَ سَعِيرًا, joining the orphan's withheld due to the fire-bearing prayer root.

luna: This command joins worship of God with goodness to orphans and needy people, then condemns arrogant self-display; it gathers the section's social duties and outward-looking failure in one address. | terra: Worship of God is joined to good treatment of orphans, the needy, near and distant neighbours, and travelers; 4:37-38 then expose withholding and display as violations of this command.

luna: The section's withheld household help meets a passage about those who are stingy and conceal God's bounty; “يَبْخَلُونَ” and “يَكْتُمُونَ” give withholding a material and hidden side. | terra: The stingy both command others to stinginess and conceal God's bounty, the precise negative counterpart to urging food and making provision available.

luna: The section makes a show-prayer image central; this neighboring description says people spend “رِئَاءَ النَّاسِ,” using the same r-ʾ-y root as the source's display word and applying it to visible giving. | terra: Spending wealth رِئَاءَ النَّاسِ is joined to disbelief in God and the Last Day, so visible giving and denial of account occupy one act.
terra: The intoxicated may not approach prayer until they know what they are saying, defining conscious speech as a boundary against prayer whose heart is absent.
terra: The command to return trusts to their owners gives the direct ethical rule for a borrowed household item and places its return under just judgment.
terra: The ruling concerning orphan women and oppressed children commands that justice be upheld for orphans, making visible the dependents whom stronger household members could overlook.

luna: This ayah joins the section's distracted prayer and its “for show” image in one description: hypocrites come to prayer lazily, “يُرَاءُونَ النَّاسَ,” and remember God only a little. | terra: When hypocrites rise to prayer lazily, يُرَاءُونَ النَّاسَ and remember God only a little; prayer, the human gaze, and the absent heart coincide exactly.
terra: The covenant joins prayer, zakat, faithful support, and a good loan to God, an explicit repaired version of the section's prayer-and-debt relation.

luna: The section depicts a hand driving the vulnerable away; this command forbids driving away people who call on their Lord morning and evening, protecting their place in the gathering. | terra: Do not drive away those who call their Lord seeking His face; their account is not yours and yours is not theirs, joining sincere worship, refusal to repel, and separate accountability.
terra: The question whether these lowly worshippers are really the ones God favored exposes the social gaze behind driving them away; 6:52 states their sincere worship and separate account.

terra: The source's Suhā-star example makes Abraham's seeing a star and then observing it set a plausible visual echo: a star is attended to rather than missed, though this ayah does not concern prayer or aid.

luna: Alongside its command for just measure, this ayah forbids approaching an orphan's property except in the best way until maturity, joining protection of the vulnerable to a measured due. | terra: Do not approach orphan property except in the best way until maturity, and give full measure and justice; the orphan's protection and the small due meet in one command.
terra: God sheltered a small, vulnerable people, strengthened them, and provided good things; the awā root joins protection and provision as in the orphan and Mary scenes.
terra: Their ṣalāt at the House is only whistling and clapping, and punishment answers their disbelief; it is another worship-form emptied of its inward act.
terra: A fixed share of acquired wealth is assigned to kin, orphans, the needy, and travelers, preventing the vulnerable recipients from disappearing at distribution.

luna: The source links display to a path cut short; this warning names those who leave home in arrogance and “رِئَاءَ النَّاسِ” while barring others from God's way, joining public display to obstruction. | terra: The army leaves home boastfully and رِئَاءَ النَّاسِ, extending the source's spectator-facing conduct from prayer and charity to a public procession.
terra: Those who gave shelter and help become mutual protectors, extending the source's shelter verb into a human protective circle.
terra: Those who gave shelter and help are declared true believers, repeating the awā shelter formulation as a human protective circle around the vulnerable.

luna: The section's ma'un includes a due in wealth and small assistance; this warning addresses those who hoard gold and silver instead of spending in God's way, extending withheld help to hoarded wealth. | terra: Those who hoard wealth and do not spend it in God's way are warned of painful punishment, joining closed wealth to the fire detailed in 9:35.

luna: The hoarding passage continues with the treasure heated in Hell and used to brand its owners; it completes the section's meeting of withheld wealth and fire with a concrete judgment scene. | terra: The hoarded metal is heated in hell and brands bodies, turning withheld wealth into the fire it has earned.

luna: The section separates empty prayer from withheld aid; this account of hypocrites puts the failures together: they approach prayer lazily and spend only reluctantly, linking ritual neglect with a closed hand. | terra: The m-n-ʿ wording "nothing prevented" their spending from acceptance sits in one ayah with disbelief, lazy prayer, and unwilling expenditure, a dense parallel to the section's broken links.

luna: The section reads al-ma'un as zakah and a due; this verse assigns zakah among the poor, needy, debtors, and other named recipients, specifying how a share reaches people who need it. | terra: Obligatory alms are assigned to the poor, needy, debtors, and other named recipients, joining māʿūn's zakat sense to its debt image through protected shares.

luna: The section says hypocritical-looking people withhold the small aid; this description of hypocrite men and women says they forbid right and “يَقْبِضُونَ أَيْدِيَهُمْ,” explicitly joining obstruction to hands held closed.

luna: Against the closed hands and obstruction of the preceding hypocrites, believing men and women help one another, establish prayer, and give zakah; the verse states the mutual circle the section says has broken.

luna: The section says the share, prayer, and reassurance form a broken circle; here the Messenger is told to take charity and pray for its givers, and “إِنَّ صَلَاتَكَ سَكَنٌ لَّهُمْ” names that prayer as their comfort. | terra: The command to take a due charity and pray over the givers makes that prayer a tranquility for them, restoring the section's broken circle of share, prayer, and inward rest.

terra: The command to act is followed by the warning that God, His messenger, and believers will see the work before return to the Knower of hidden and visible, setting public gaze inside final accounting.

luna: The chiefs reject Noah's followers as the lowest people and say they see no distinction in them; this scene explicitly stages the social gaze that discounts the lowly whom the section says are passed over.
luna: Noah answers that he will not drive away the believers; the verse directly reverses the section's pushing away of the vulnerable and says those believers will meet their Lord.
luna: Noah asks who would protect him from God if he drove the believers away; this continuation ties refusal to expel the lowly to the protection image developed around the orphan.
luna: Noah refuses to declare that those whom people's eyes scorn will receive no good from God; this directly challenges the section's way of overlooking the dim and vulnerable.
terra: No mountain can shelter Noah's son from the flood: his attempted refuge and overwhelming water form the failed boundary opposite the secure high resting place and flowing water of 23:50.
terra: The water-drawer lowers his bucket into the well, giving a concrete Quranic scene for the source's dictionary sense of māʿūn as a bucket, though the narrative is rescue rather than lending.
terra: Those seeking their Lord's face establish prayer and spend secretly and openly, and their reward is the final Home; gaze, prayer, provision, and dwelling are rejoined.
terra: Believers are told to establish prayer and spend secretly and openly before a Day with no trade or friendship, placing both visible and hidden giving under account.
terra: Giving kin, the needy, and the traveler their due states the positive obligation corresponding to the share withheld as māʿūn.

luna: The section's dictionary gloss includes a tight-handed person; this command pictures the hand chained to the neck and forbids that restraint, setting generosity between withholding and waste. | terra: The concrete image of a hand chained to the neck marks the boundary of stinginess, while the warning against total extension keeps giving responsible.

luna: This repeated command likewise forbids approaching an orphan's property except in the best way until maturity; it makes the lost-guardian image concrete as a continuing duty to safeguard the child's resources. | terra: Protection of orphan property until maturity is joined to fulfilling the covenant because covenants are questioned, placing guardianship under account.

luna: This command says to stay with those who call on their Lord and not let one's eyes pass beyond them for worldly adornment; it meets the section's eyes-for-people image with a direct boundary on whom to keep in view. | terra: The command not to let one's eyes pass beyond sincere worshippers toward worldly adornment directly reverses overlooking the socially faint and following a heedless heart.
terra: The record leaves neither small nor large uncounted and presents every deed, making the section's smallest withheld aid part of the denied account.
terra: The town refuses the travelers hospitality, yet a collapsing wall is repaired there; 18:82 reveals that the wall shelters orphan property.

luna: The section's shelter image meets the story of a wall built for two orphans so their treasure remains protected until they mature; the verse makes hidden, future provision a reason to preserve a place for children. | terra: The repaired wall protects treasure belonging to two orphan boys until maturity because their father was righteous, materially restoring the protective ring around orphan property.
terra: Successors who neglected prayer and followed desires will meet ruin, giving a direct outcome for prayer allowed to lapse.

luna: The section contrasts prayer for people's eyes with prayer's inward purpose; God commands prayer “لِذِكْرِي,” for His remembrance, giving the act a different addressee and aim. | terra: أَقِمِ الصَّلَاةَ لِذِكْرِي states remembrance as prayer's purpose, the direct inward answer to being heedless of one's prayer.
terra: The command not to stretch one's eyes toward worldly display restrains the very gaze that misses the lowly; 20:132 redirects the household to prayer and divine provision.
terra: Command the household to prayer and persist in it; God asks no provision but provides, joining home, sustained worship, and provision without display.
terra: The just scales for Resurrection allow no wrong, and even a mustard-seed weight is brought forward, linking precise repayment to the small due.

luna: The section's prayer is empty and performed for an audience; this passage marks the successful believers by humility “فِي صَلَاتِهِمْ خَاشِعُونَ,” a direct reversal in the prayer itself. | terra: The successful believers are inwardly humble in prayer, supplying the heart-attention missing from the section's outward prayer.

luna: The same profile continues by giving zakah, turning the section's withheld al-ma'un into an active duty within a sound prayerful life. | terra: The same portrait makes them active in zakat, keeping prayer and the due share joined.
terra: They guard trusts and covenants, a direct ethic for the borrowed object that māʿūn can denote; 23:9 then returns to prayer.

luna: The profile ends this list by guarding its prayers; that care reverses the section's people who let prayer slip from their attention. | terra: They carefully guard their prayers, closing the trust-and-prayer sequence with the opposite of sahw.

luna: The section notes the same shelter verb for Mary and her son: “وَآوَيْنَاهُمَا” gives them refuge, while “قَرَارٍ وَمَعِينٍ” joins settled shelter to a flowing spring, meeting its home-and-water image. | terra: The source's dictionary water sense of māʿūn meets مَعِين here, while آوَيْنَاهُمَا places Mary and her son in a secure resting place beside flowing water.

luna: The section shows people withholding small help; this verse tells people of means not to swear off giving to relatives, the needy, and migrants, and urges pardon, directly reversing the closed hand. | terra: People of means must not swear to stop giving kin, the needy, and emigrants, a direct prohibition on turning grievance into withheld aid.

luna: The section's men pray for human eyes; here trade does not distract the believers from God's remembrance, prayer, and zakah, and they fear a Day when hearts and eyes turn over, a specific inward-facing counter-image. | terra: People whom trade does not distract from remembrance, prayer, and zakat fear a Day when hearts and eyes overturn; inward attention, share, account, and sight remain joined.
terra: Permission to eat from relatives' and friends' houses portrays household food and access as socially shared, a broad but concrete opposite to the closed shelf and door.
terra: Prayer, zakat, and certainty in the Hereafter form one positive triad, the intact opposite of heedless prayer, withheld māʿūn, and denial of dīn.
terra: At the water of Midian, two women hold their flock back while others draw, staging vulnerable people waiting at access to water.
terra: Moses waters for the two women without demanding return, a small act of water-aid that reverses withholding māʿūn.
terra: Giving kin, the needy, and the traveler their due is tied to seeking God's face, uniting the protected share with intention free of human display.
terra: The same prayer-zakat-certainty triad recurs as the identifying practice of those who do good, reinforcing the section's linked rather than separated obedience.
terra: Even a mustard-seed weight hidden in rock or anywhere else is brought by God, a nonvisual parallel to the faint person and small deed that human sight misses.
terra: The transgressors' مَأْوَاهُمُ النَّارُ is a fire-abode from which they are returned whenever they try to leave, and they are told it is the fire they denied.
terra: Large basins and fixed cauldrons are made for David's household, followed by "work in gratitude"; the source's dictionary pot sense becomes an implement of grateful service.
terra: Prayer and spending secretly and openly are joined to hope for a transaction that never fails, opposing display and withheld provision under a lasting account.
terra: When commanded to spend from God's provision, the disbelievers ask whether they should feed someone God could feed, joining refusal of food to unbelief.
terra: A cup مِن مَعِينٍ brings a vessel and the source's flowing-water sense of māʿūn into one compact image.
terra: God knows the stealthy glance and what breasts conceal, joining the section's field of human looking to the inward heart that outward prayer misses.
terra: Those who refuse zakat are identified in the same ayah as disbelievers in the Hereafter, directly joining the withheld due to denial of account.
terra: Golden dishes and cups are passed around while their contents delight the eyes, joining household vessels, circulation rather than withholding, and the image of sight.

luna: The section says its actors want not to be overlooked while denying the Day; after such people forget their meeting with that Day, this verse says they will be forgotten and their refuge is the Fire, a direct reversal of their wish to remain seen.
terra: Some who are called to spend withhold, but their stinginess is against themselves; the ayah explicitly turns refused provision back upon the withholder.
terra: مَنَّاعٍ لِلْخَيْرِ names the condemned person as an emphatic preventer of good, the same m-n-ʿ character embodied by withholding māʿūn.

luna: The section develops “سَاهُونَ” (root s-h-w) as heedlessness in the field of seeing; this verse uses the same form for people in heedlessness, and its following question is about the Day of Judgment. | terra: فِي غَمْرَةٍ سَاهُونَ is the other pointed Quranic use of the source's s-h-w root: heedlessness becomes an engulfing depth rather than mere distraction in prayer.

luna: The section joins prayer-neglect to denial of reckoning; continuing the “heedless” description, this verse asks “أَيَّانَ يَوْمُ الدِّينِ,” putting their heedlessness beside the very day they dispute. | terra: The heedless people of 51:11 ask when the Day of Account will be, joining their inattention to the reckoning denied in the section.
terra: The answer places those heedless questioners over the fire for trial, continuing the section's move from sahw to fire.
terra: They are told to taste the trial they sought to hasten, completing 51:11-13's heedlessness-account-fire sequence.
luna: Against the section's prayer performed for onlookers, the God-fearing in this passage sleep little at night; this quiet, unseen discipline is a specific opposite to worship staged for people.
luna: The same night-devotion passage says they ask forgiveness before dawn; this private turning toward God contrasts with the section's prayer whose heart is absent and audience is human.

luna: The section understands small aid as a due in wealth; this verse says the God-fearing have “حَقٌّ مَّعْلُومٌ” in their property for the asker and deprived, joining inner devotion to a specified right for others. | terra: A due for the asker and deprived is present in their wealth, the compact counterpart of 70:24-25 and the opposite of withholding the small share.
terra: The woe pronounced on the deniers begins the short sequence that reaches pushing and fire in 52:13-14, matching the source's movement from denial to woe.
terra: The deniers are immersed in playful خَوْض immediately before being pushed, a close counterpart to heedless immersion before reckoning; 52:13 gives its destination.

luna: The section explicitly links the orphan-pushing verb in 107:2 to fire: here the same root, د-ع-ع, is used as people are driven “إِلَىٰ نَارِ جَهَنَّمَ,” making the treatment rebound on its actors. | terra: يُدَعُّونَ إِلَى نَارِ جَهَنَّمَ دَعًّا uses the same d-ʿ-ʿ root as the source's violent pushing of the orphan, but the push now drives the denier into fire.

luna: The section pairs denial with fire; this ayah calls it “هَٰذِهِ النَّارُ” that they had denied, making the denied consequence present before them. | terra: هَذِهِ النَّارُ الَّتِي كُنْتُمْ بِهَا تُكَذِّبُونَ explicitly identifies the fire toward which 52:13 pushes them as the fire they denied.
terra: After the deniers are pushed to the fire they denied, the question whether it is magic or they cannot see adds the section's seeing motif to that exact push-fire scene.
terra: Everything people have done is in written records, corresponding to the account that outward display cannot evade.
terra: Every small and great thing is inscribed, giving the smallness of māʿūn full weight within that account.
terra: أَكْوَابٍ وَأَبَارِيقَ وَكَأْسٍ مِن مَعِينٍ gathers cups, ewers, and flowing drink, directly staging the vessel-and-water meanings that the section places inside one word.

luna: The section's dictionary sense of ma'un includes a small loan; this repeated Quranic image asks who will give God “قَرْضًا حَسَنًا,” extending the domestic lending image to wealth entrusted for God's reward.
terra: Charitable men and women are described as lending God a good loan that is multiplied, converting the section's withheld small debt into freely offered aid.
terra: Distribution is assigned to kin, orphans, the needy, and the traveler so wealth does not circulate only among the rich, turning the small withheld share into a protected social right.
terra: Those settled in the Home welcome migrants and prefer them despite their own need; the open dwelling and conquest of inner stinginess reverse the closed house of māʿūn.
terra: When people see trade or diversion they rush toward it and leave the speaker standing; the eye abandons worship for visible provision while God's provision is declared better.
terra: Wealth and children must not distract believers from remembrance; this gives a specific worldly form to the absent attention that the section finds in prayer.
terra: The next command is to spend before death makes the person plead for delay to give charity, joining distraction to aid withheld until too late.
terra: The command to hear, obey, and spend is paired with deliverance from the soul's stinginess, opposing the hand that withholds māʿūn.

luna: The section's dictionary sense of ma'un includes a small loan; this verse likewise says “تُقْرِضُوا اللَّهَ قَرْضًا حَسَنًا,” carrying that lending image into giving that God multiplies and forgives. | terra: A good loan to God follows the command to spend and is multiplied and forgiven, converting the debt image into willing generosity.
terra: The question asks who could provide if God withheld His provision, a direct divine-scale counterpart to the human hand that withholds a small provided good.
terra: قُلْ أَرَأَيْتُمْ asks the reader to look, then imagines water disappearing and asks who can bring مَاءٍ مَعِينٍ; sight, hidden provision, and the source's flowing-water sense converge.
terra: مَنَّاعٍ لِلْخَيْرِ again fixes the tight-fisted character in the source's m-n-ʿ root, now within a portrait of public moral corruption.
terra: The garden owners are introduced as a test case of people planning a harvest; 68:24-25 disclose that their plan is to exclude the poor.
terra: A visitation destroys the garden while they sleep, making hidden judgment answer the hidden plan to withhold the poor person's food.
terra: The garden owners whisper that no poor person should enter upon them that day, turning overlooked need into a deliberate closed-door policy.
terra: They set out early intent on withholding, making the refusal of the poor person's food an organized act; 68:24 states its target.
terra: The garden owners realize that they themselves have been deprived, a pointed reversal of their plan in 68:24-25 to deprive the poor person.

luna: The section connects the failure to urge food with a fire sentence; the account orders, “ثُمَّ الْجَحِيمَ صَلُّوهُ,” turning that same person's reckoning into punishment. | terra: ثُمَّ الْجَحِيمَ صَلُّوهُ supplies the fire sense carried by the section's ṣ-l-y/ṣ-l-w wordplay on "those who pray."

luna: The source cites the same person's fire-account at 69:31; this continuation specifies that he is bound in a chain, carrying the punishment scene forward before the account names his neglected duties.

luna: In the same reckoning invoked by the section, this ayah names the person's failure to believe in God before the next verse names the poor he did not feed; it joins denied faith to denied care. | terra: The person sent to fire did not believe in God; this ayah supplies the denial immediately before 69:34 identifies his failure to urge feeding the poor.

luna: The section directly links fire to failure to urge food; this ayah repeats “لَا يَحُضُّ عَلَىٰ طَعَامِ الْمِسْكِينِ,” with the same ḥ-ḍ-ḍ root as its source wording, in that condemned man's account. | terra: وَلَا يَحُضُّ عَلَى طَعَامِ الْمِسْكِينِ repeats the rare wording about not urging the feeding of the poor and gives the reason for 69:31's fire.
terra: The condemned person has no close protector there, extending the source's broken protective circle around the vulnerable; 69:34 states his failure toward the poor.
terra: His only food is foul discharge, a punitive reversal of the food he would not urge for the poor in 69:34 and of the household hearth developed in the section.

luna: The section's withholding root appears in this portrait: when good reaches a person, he is “مَنُوعًا,” showing the same m-n-ʿ restraint that culminates in withholding al-ma'un. | terra: مَنُوعًا names the human being as intensely withholding when good reaches him, the same m-n-ʿ disposition embodied in withholding māʿūn.

luna: The section sets hollow prayer against a real devotional circle; after describing the withholding person, this passage exempts “الْمُصَلِّينَ,” the worshippers who answer that tendency. | terra: إِلَّا الْمُصَلِّينَ begins the explicit exception to the withholding person of 70:21 and opens the intact circle that surah 107 breaks.

luna: The section's false prayer is bounded by people who remain constant in prayer: “عَلَىٰ صَلَاتِهِمْ دَائِمُونَ” describes continuing worship rather than prayer that is neglected. | terra: Those excepted are constant in their prayer, directly reversing prayer from which the heart has wandered.

luna: The section glosses al-ma'un as a due; this ayah says such people have “حَقٌّ مَّعْلُومٌ” in their wealth, making giving a recognized right rather than optional display. | terra: Their wealth contains a مَعْلُومٌ حَقٌّ, turning the withheld small due into an acknowledged and measured right.

luna: The preceding known right is for “السَّائِلِ وَالْمَحْرُومِ”; this continuation identifies the very claimant and deprived person whom the section's withheld help leaves unseen. | terra: The known right is for both the asker and the deprived, specifying the overlooked poor person who receives it.

luna: The section begins with people denying the Day of Recompense; the same devotional profile says they “يُصَدِّقُونَ بِيَوْمِ الدِّينِ,” making belief in that day part of the repaired circle. | terra: They affirm the Day of Account, completing the exact reversal of denial, neglected prayer, and withheld property across 70:21-26.
terra: Those who affirm the Day in 70:26 also fear their Lord's punishment, showing the inward force that keeps prayer and the poor person's known right intact.
terra: Within the same Meʿāric portrait, the worshippers guard trusts and covenants, extending the known financial right to borrowed or entrusted things.
terra: They guard their prayers, closing the longer sequence begun with constancy in prayer and containing the known right and affirmed account.

luna: The section's dictionary sense of ma'un includes a small loan; this verse asks for a good loan to God, placing material giving within the obedient service that the section joins to al-ma'un. | terra: Prayer and zakat stand beside lending God a good loan, so the section's worship, due share, and debt image meet as willing obedience.

luna: The section says the images return as one confession from inside the fire; this is the question that frames it: “مَا سَلَكَكُمْ فِي سَقَرَ,” asking the condemned what led them there. | terra: The question مَا سَلَكَكُمْ فِي سَقَرَ opens the fire-side confession in which the section's prayer, food, heedlessness, and denied account are gathered.

luna: The source's empty, outward prayer returns as a confession: “لَمْ نَكُ مِنَ الْمُصَلِّينَ.” The inmates themselves name the missing prayer among the causes of their being in Saqar. | terra: The answer "we were not among those who prayed" supplies the failed-prayer member of the confession opened in 74:42.

luna: The section's closed mouth around the poor's meal returns as “لَمْ نَكُ نُطْعِمُ الْمِسْكِينَ”; their confession turns withheld feeding into an acknowledged cause of the fire. | terra: The confessors say that they did not feed the poor, reproducing the section's neglected miskīn as one cause of Sakar.

luna: The section's gloss “gaflete dalmak” meets this confession of “نَخُوضُ مَعَ الْخَائِضِينَ”: they went along with those who indulged, adding shared heedlessness to the private failures. | terra: Their joining those who plunged into vain talk gives the confession its heedless immersion, corresponding to the section's missed heart in prayer; 74:43-46 specify the whole sequence.

luna: The section starts from denial of the reckoning; the inmates say “نُكَذِّبُ بِيَوْمِ الدِّينِ,” using the same k-dh-b root as 107:1 to state that denial from inside the fire. | terra: وَكُنَّا نُكَذِّبُ بِيَوْمِ الدِّينِ closes the confessed sequence with the same denial of the Day of Account that opens surah 107.

luna: The section presents the preceding answers as the account of how they reached the fire; their next words say this continued “حَتَّىٰ أَتَانَا الْيَقِينُ,” giving the confession its endpoint in death.
terra: فَلَا صَدَّقَ وَلَا صَلَّى pairs refusal to affirm with refusal to pray, setting up the denial and turning away in 75:32.
terra: وَلَكِن كَذَّبَ وَتَوَلَّى repeats the denial-and-turning pair of 96:13 as the explanation of not praying in 75:31.

luna: The section shows a meal withheld from the poor; this passage reverses the act by feeding the needy, orphan, and captive, making practical care the visible counterpart to withholding. | terra: They feed the poor, orphan, and captive despite loving the food, reversing both the pushed orphan and food withheld from the needy.

luna: The section's worshippers seek human notice; these givers say they feed only for God's face and seek neither reward nor thanks, clarifying the intention that the source's show-prayer lacks. | terra: They feed solely for God's face and seek neither repayment nor thanks, directly opposing an act arranged for spectators or social return.

luna: The same givers say they fear a frowning, difficult day from their Lord; this continues the reversal of those who deny the reckoning at the heart of the section. | terra: Their fear of a harsh Day supplies the affirmed account behind the sincere feeding in 76:8-9.
terra: Silver vessels and cups circulate as the reward of the sincere feeders, reversing the household vessel withheld as māʿūn.
terra: The crystal-silver vessels are measured precisely, adding exact measure to the freely circulating household ware of 76:15.

luna: The section joins being overlooked with wanting to be seen; this ayah opens a scene with a person turning away, and the continuation reveals that his attention had gone to the self-sufficient while a vulnerable visitor waited. | terra: The frown and turning away bodily enact the section's skipped weak person and begin a sustained correction of misplaced attention.

luna: This continuation identifies the arriving person as blind; the section's missed orphan and poor similarly stand at the edge of another's attention, though this ayah's visitor is not said to be poor. | terra: The person passed over is blind, making the ethics of seeing and being unseen concrete.

luna: The section says the person looked past can contain an unseen inner life; this continuation asks whether the blind visitor might become purified, making his potential a reason not to dismiss him. | terra: The overlooked blind visitor may purify himself, showing the inward value missed by the gaze that turns toward the self-sufficient.

luna: The same visitor might remember and benefit from a reminder; this adds the possible spiritual benefit that the neglecting gaze in the section fails to see. | terra: He may receive a reminder that benefits him, specifying what is lost when attention skips him.

luna: The section's vulnerable people are passed over while its actors seek notice; the next figure in this scene is one who considers himself self-sufficient, the socially powerful person whose attention draws the gaze. | terra: The self-sufficient person is the one granted attention, corresponding to those who demand not to be passed over.

luna: This ayah says attention is directed toward that self-sufficient figure; it identifies where the gaze went in the scene of overlooking the blind visitor. | terra: فَأَنتَ لَهُ تَصَدَّى says attention is actively directed toward the self-sufficient person, sharpening the unequal distribution of the gaze.

luna: The passage bounds the preacher's responsibility by saying he is not accountable if the self-sufficient man refuses purification; that distinction helps keep the section's failure of care separate from the recipient's response. | terra: The addressee is not accountable for the self-sufficient person's refusal to purify himself, undercutting the impulse to give that person preferential attention.

luna: The passage turns to another arrival, one who comes striving; this keeps the focus on the person who actively seeks attention after the well-positioned figure received it. | terra: The other person comes striving, so his low visibility cannot be confused with lack of inward purpose.

luna: This arriving person fears God; the detail makes his inward seriousness visible in the very scene where the gaze is diverted from him. | terra: The overlooked seeker comes in fear, adding inward reverence to the striving named in 80:8 before he is neglected in 80:10.

luna: The ayah says attention is diverted from the striving, God-fearing arrival; this is the same specific failure of sight and attention developed by the section's overlooked vulnerable people. | terra: فَأَنتَ عَنْهُ تَلَهَّى names distraction from that sincere seeker, closely paralleling the source's attention that skips the dim person and prayer's heart.
terra: كَلَّا بَلْ تُكَذِّبُونَ بِالدِّينِ repeats denial of dīn and immediately opens a scene of uninterrupted observation and recording.
terra: وَإِنَّ عَلَيْكُمْ لَحَافِظِينَ places guardians continually over those who deny account, echoing the gaze that never leaves.
terra: The guardians are noble scribes, converting unseen observation into the written account denied in 82:9.
terra: يَعْلَمُونَ مَا تَفْعَلُونَ states that the observers know the deeds, including the small acts people overlook or perform for other eyes.
terra: يَصْلَوْنَهَا يَوْمَ الدِّينِ puts the fire verb and the Day of Account in one line after 82:9-12's denial and surveillance.
terra: وَمَا هُمْ عَنْهَا بِغَائِبِينَ says they cannot be absent from that fire, reversing the attempt to let the poor or one's own prayer fall out of sight.
terra: The Day of Account culminates when no soul controls anything for another and command belongs to God, defining the final settlement behind 82:9-18.

luna: The section reads al-ma'un as a small obligation; this warning concerns people who short the measure, a concrete case of withholding what another is due. | terra: وَيْلٌ لِلْمُطَفِّفِينَ moves the section's woe into the marketplace, where a small due is withheld rather than a small household aid.

luna: The section says the person denies another's small right yet seeks not to be overlooked; this ayah specifies the asymmetry: he takes full measure when receiving from others. | terra: The defrauders demand full measure when receiving from people, matching the section's people who insist that they themselves not be skipped.

luna: Continuing that asymmetry, the trader gives others less in the scale; the section's withheld aid and performed self-importance meet here as giving less while expecting full treatment. | terra: When they measure for others they diminish the due, a transactional form of withholding māʿūn.

luna: The section links denied dues with denial of a reckoning; the measure-fraud passage next asks whether these people think they will be raised, making the ethical accounting answerable to a final one. | terra: The question whether such people expect resurrection joins the apparently small withheld amount to accountability.

luna: The same question specifies “لِيَوْمٍ عَظِيمٍ”; this continues the reckoning frame that the section joins to the withheld small right. | terra: The resurrection is specified as a tremendous Day, enlarging the moral weight of the small shortage in 83:2-3.

luna: The passage concludes that all people stand before the Lord of the worlds; that scene gives the section's contrast between being seen by people and answerable to God a concrete endpoint. | terra: People stand before the Lord on that Day, replacing the customers' gaze with the final divine accounting of the unequal exchange.
terra: The record of the wicked is introduced immediately after the short measure and resurrection scene, making the small withheld due a written matter of account.
terra: The question asking what can convey the nature of Sijjīn interrupts complacent vision and directs attention to the record named around it.
terra: A written register completes 83:7-8, corresponding to the accounting that captures the small shortage of 83:2-3.
terra: Another woe falls on the deniers, linking the commercial withholding of 83:1-3 to the source's denial-and-woe movement.
terra: الَّذِينَ يُكَذِّبُونَ بِيَوْمِ الدِّينِ names the object of their denial as the Day of Account.
terra: The deniers are veiled from their Lord before entering fire in 83:16, turning the section's seeing-and-being-seen field into a punitive loss of sight or access.
terra: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُمْ لَصَالُوا الْجَحِيمِ gives the fire-bearing ṣ-l-y outcome of the denial named in 83:11.
terra: وَيَصْلَى سَعِيرًا begins a compact sequence in which fire, the household, denial of return, and God's seeing converge.
terra: The fire-bound person had been joyful among his own household, bringing the home into the accountability sequence of 84:12-15.
terra: He supposed he would never return, expressing the denial of final accounting beneath his ease at home.
terra: إِنَّ رَبَّهُ كَانَ بِهِ بَصِيرًا answers that denial with the Lord's constant seeing, exactly as 96:14 answers performative prayer.

luna: The section's dictionary image calls Suhā too faint to notice; the night sky's “النَّجْمُ الثَّاقِبُ” is instead a piercing star, a specific brightness reversal that makes the overlooked star's faintness salient.
terra: الَّذِي يَصْلَى النَّارَ الْكُبْرَى gives the fire side of the section's prayer/fire word meeting only three ayat before actual prayer.
terra: The one in that fire neither dies nor lives, spelling out the endured consequence attached to the fire verb in 87:12.
terra: قَدْ أَفْلَحَ مَن تَزَكَّى turns from the fire-bound person to purification, preparing the genuine prayer of 87:15 and recalling māʿūn as zakat.
terra: وَذَكَرَ اسْمَ رَبِّهِ فَصَلَّى answers 87:12's fire-bearing form with remembered, God-directed prayer rather than prayer emptied of attention.
terra: Faces enter a blazing fire with the ṣ-l-y verb; the following ayat turn immediately to drink and food, making this a compact fire-hearth reversal.
terra: They drink from a boiling spring, a punitive joining of water and the fire scene in 88:4 rather than the sheltering flowing water of 23:50.
terra: They have no food except a thorny plant that neither nourishes nor relieves hunger, the negative endpoint of refusing food to the needy.
terra: A flowing spring in the garden reverses the punitive spring of 88:5 and supplies the water side of the section's māʿūn image.
terra: Cups are set ready beside that garden scene, bringing available vessels together with flowing water rather than withholding them.

luna: The section says the dim, vulnerable orphan is passed over; this rebuke states “لَا تُكْرِمُونَ الْيَتِيمَ,” naming failure to honor the orphan as the very social fault at issue. | terra: كَلَّا بَل لَا تُكْرِمُونَ الْيَتِيمَ gives the direct social failure toward the orphan whose continuation is failure to urge feeding in 89:18.

luna: Where the source says the person does not urge food for the poor, this ayah says “وَلَا تَحَاضُّونَ عَلَىٰ طَعَامِ الْمِسْكِينِ,” repeating the h-ḍ-ḍ root as a communal failure to encourage feeding. | terra: وَلَا تَحَاضُّونَ عَلَى طَعَامِ الْمِسْكِينِ closely repeats the section's rare urging-food construction immediately after neglect of the orphan.

luna: The section pairs neglect of the orphan with withholding small aid; the next charge in this same rebuke is consuming inheritance “أَكْلًا لَّمًّا,” extending the scene to taking what should be protected.

luna: The section links overlooked people with a hand that withholds; this continuation says the people “تُحِبُّونَ الْمَالَ حُبًّا جَمًّا,” naming attachment to wealth alongside the neglected orphan and poor.
terra: Hell is brought forth on the Day in the same surah that has condemned failure toward the orphan and failure to urge feeding the poor, supplying their eventual fire horizon.

luna: Where the section says no one urges food for the poor, this passage makes feeding during famine a passage through hardship, reversing neglect with a concrete act of provision. | terra: Feeding on a day of hunger is named as the hard ascent, turning the mouth that does not urge food into a costly act of provision.

luna: The next detail specifies that the hungry one is an orphan “ذَا مَقْرَبَةٍ,” closely joining food to care for the vulnerable child in the section. | terra: The first recipient is an orphan of kin, joining feeding to restoration of the orphan's lost protective circle.

luna: The continuing list names a needy person “ذَا مَتْرَبَةٍ”; it makes visible the socially lowly person whom the section says is overlooked. | terra: The second recipient is a needy person in dust, making visible the socially low person the source says is easily missed.
luna: The section's person does not encourage feeding; this passage praises believers who “تَوَاصَوْا بِالْمَرْحَمَةِ,” urging one another to mercy and forming a supportive circle.
terra: لَا يَصْلَاهَا إِلَّا الْأَشْقَى introduces fire with the same ṣ-l-y form that the section hears beneath the name of prayer.
terra: The fire-bound person is الَّذِي كَذَّبَ وَتَوَلَّى, reproducing denial and turning away before the passage contrasts him with a giver.
terra: The Godfearing person is kept away from the fire before 92:18 describes his purifying gift, completing the passage's reversal of denial, turning away, and fire.
terra: The Godfearing person gives his wealth to purify himself, reversing both withholding and spectator-facing devotion.
terra: His gift is not repayment for a favor owed to anyone, clarifying that the giving is free of the social debt and gaze the section exposes.
terra: إِلَّا ابْتِغَاءَ وَجْهِ رَبِّهِ الْأَعْلَى makes the Lord's face alone the aim of the giver in 92:18, the sharpest opposite of human-directed display.

luna: The section identifies the shelter verb for the orphan here: “فَآوَىٰ” says God found the addressee orphaned and gave him refuge, the protective act opposite the pushed-away child. | terra: أَلَمْ يَجِدْكَ يَتِيمًا فَآوَى answers the pushed orphan with God's finding and sheltering; its آوى also leads to the water-shelter meeting in 23:50.

luna: The section shows a hand pushing the orphan away; “فَلَا تَقْهَرِ الْيَتِيمَ” reverses that act with a direct command not to oppress the orphan. | terra: فَأَمَّا الْيَتِيمَ فَلَا تَقْهَرْ turns God's shelter in 93:6 into a command never to dominate or repel the orphan.

luna: Beside the command about the orphan, “فَلَا تَنْهَرِ السَّائِلَ” forbids driving off a petitioner; it reverses the source section's refusal to open the way to a needy person. | terra: وَأَمَّا السَّائِلَ فَلَا تَنْهَرْ forbids rebuffing the asker at the door, the direct ethical reverse of denying small aid.

luna: The section says the Al-Alaq scene opens with its own “Have you seen”; this ayah opens that scene with “أَرَأَيْتَ,” echoing the source section's seeing question while turning sight toward a person who obstructs prayer. | terra: أَرَأَيْتَ الَّذِي يَنْهَى repeats the section's demand to look and directs that look toward a person obstructing worship.

luna: The section says the Al-Alaq scene brings prayer into the meeting: this continuation identifies the obstructed one as “عَبْدًا إِذَا صَلَّىٰ,” making the blocked act explicit. | terra: عَبْدًا إِذَا صَلَّى identifies what is being stopped: a servant in the act of prayer, making the path in 96:9 physically and spiritually interrupted.

luna: The section says the Al-Alaq scene adds a path interrupted midway; the next conditional asks whether the praying servant was “عَلَى الْهُدَىٰ,” giving that path a specific direction toward guidance. | terra: The second أَرَأَيْتَ asks whether the praying servant is upon guidance, adding the half-blocked way named in the section to 96:9-10.

luna: The source's interrupted way also has an ethical destination: this continuation asks whether the servant “أَمَرَ بِالتَّقْوَىٰ,” so the obstruction reaches beyond the prayer act to a call to heed God. | terra: The possibility that the servant commands taqwā makes his interrupted prayer an inwardly directed act, unlike prayer performed for spectators.

luna: The source section brings denial and turning away into its account of false religion; this ayah asks whether the obstructer “كَذَّبَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ,” joining denial to withdrawal in the same prayer-blocking scene. | terra: أَرَأَيْتَ إِن كَذَّبَ وَتَوَلَّى joins looking, denial, and bodily turning away in the very scene of obstructed prayer.

luna: The section sets public looking against the wish not to be overlooked; the scene closes, “بِأَنَّ اللَّهَ يَرَىٰ,” with God's sight as the boundary on human display. | terra: أَلَمْ يَعْلَمْ بِأَنَّ اللَّهَ يَرَى makes God's unbroken seeing the answer to worship arranged for human eyes.

luna: The section's show-prayer is bounded by the command to worship God with sincere devotion, establish prayer, and give zakah; this verse joins the same acts under “مُخْلِصِينَ لَهُ الدِّينَ.” | terra: Sincere worship, prayer, zakat, and دِينُ الْقَيِّمَة stand together here as the intact obedience whose pieces the section shows separated.
terra: Whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, joining the smallest helpful act to eventual seeing and account.
terra: Whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it, ensuring that even a tiny refusal hidden behind public prayer is not missed.
terra: Woe opens a portrait of public contempt and accumulated wealth that ends with fire reaching inward hearts, echoing the section's woe and surface-versus-heart concern.
terra: The condemned person amasses wealth and repeatedly counts it, a concrete closed-store counterpart to the small share or object that should circulate.
terra: The accumulated-wealth portrait reaches God's kindled fire, joining hoarding to the fire consequence developed in the section.
terra: That fire rises over the hearts, turning the inward center neglected in outward worship into the point reached by judgment.
